slides.1: Prosperity is remarkably good at hiding hardship, which is why my first question is uncomfortable. Does poverty still exist in a developed Taiwan, or have we been conditioned not to notice it?
slides.2: Ending poverty in all of its forms is the first global goal, and that wording deliberately reaches past household income. It covers housing, protection and access, so poverty is framed as a structural condition rather than a personal fault.
slides.3: Taiwan has excellent schools, health care for everyone and world-class technology, and yet inequality here has proved stubborn. A household can look completely normal while carrying debt, nursing a sick relative, or living on work that could vanish tomorrow.
slides.4: Working poverty unsettles us because it breaks the promise that effort brings security. Parents trapped in temporary contracts give up the attention their children need, and the disadvantage is passed on, quietly, to the next generation.
slides.5: What housing quietly does is eliminate everything else a family might have bought, because an unaffordable rent comes out first. Students who move house often or share a crowded room lose sleep, concentration and the confidence that classrooms reward.
slides.6: Digital participation has become a precondition for opportunity rather than a convenience. A student without a working device, a stable connection and help at home is shut out of homework, research and artificial intelligence.
slides.7: Taiwan's protective net is genuinely broad: National Health Insurance, social welfare, emergency relief and local service centers. Only when help is easy to find will it reach the household that needs it before the crisis arrives.
slides.8: Schools matter enormously because they see students every single day, which no welfare office could manage. Free meals, scholarships, counseling and supervised study take real weight off a household, and an alert teacher becomes the bridge to community help.
slides.9: Civil society reaches the households that the official system overlooks, providing food, tutoring, daily care and job information. SDG 1, however, is not an argument for charity, because the aim is capability and dignity rather than dependence.
slides.10: Financial literacy offers a modest but real form of personal power, covering budgets, savings, debt, insurance and the recognition of fraud. It cannot substitute for a decent wage, though it does tend to strengthen resilience against a sudden shock.
slides.11: Careful analysis can expose the hardship that an average hides, letting students map where services, transport and after-school help run out. Communities can then aim their money well, provided we remember that each data point is a real person.
slides.12: Service learning turns an abstract target into something actually done: interviews with social workers, guides written in two languages, hours in a tutoring program. English tends to improve under those conditions, because the language finally serves a real purpose.
slides.13: An aging society is shifting poverty towards older citizens, especially those who live alone, manage illness, or give up on services that have moved online. SDG 1 therefore connects welfare, transport, health care and the strength of local relationships.
slides.14: For migrant workers and new immigrant families, entitlement and access are split by language, paperwork and official habit. Help that cannot be understood is help that does not exist, so inclusion has to be clear, multilingual and respectful.
slides.15: Climate change acts as an inequality multiplier, because the same flood hits two homes very differently, depending on savings and insurance. Adaptation is poverty policy, and shelters, advice and local networks must exist before the emergency arrives.
slides.16: Dignity deserves treatment as a design principle rather than a courtesy, since help delivered with contempt is often refused. People in poverty are disadvantaged rather than lacking, and support built with them works better than support built for them.
slides.17: The overall position is encouraging without being anything like sufficient, because the institutions exist and the coverage is broad. What is still missing is access, timing and the fairness with which help actually reaches the households that need it.
slides.18: Perhaps the most powerful reform available to us is vocabulary, because calling people lazy ends the analysis at once. Asking instead which obstacles they meet forces a serious conversation about wages, rent, health care, transport and education.
slides.19: Students often underestimate their own power: bilingual campaigns, volunteer work, stories, simple tools, a talk given in front of a real audience. PechaKucha turns private study into public argument, which is exactly what a democracy needs.
slides.20: Eliminating poverty sounds impossibly large, yet every credible version begins locally, by noticing a need, checking the facts, speaking with respect and working with other people. A fair future begins with whatever this generation decides is worth noticing today.
